rationale: B wins because it turns the weak spots into the actual strategy instead of decorating around them. Its best line is the useful knife: "This angle dies on contact if \"up to 70%\" turns out to describe one merchant's best month." A has good bones, but it lets hype sneak onto the page with "FedNow just got its most significant commercial test" and the invented competitive flourish around Stripe and Adyen.
gaps_in_A: "FedNow just got its most significant commercial test" is an unsupported superlative. The update says Plaid uses FedNow rails; it does not prove market significance.
"competing simultaneously with Stripe and Adyen" invents a competitive frame not supplied in the update. That belongs in proof-needed, not the angle premise.
"Plaid spent a decade building the data pipes. Now it wants to own the payment." is a nice line, but it smuggles in company history and strategic intent the facts do not give you.
A misses the sharper bank-side tension B found: whether the financial institutions Plaid connects to benefit from or lose out when Pay by Bank bypasses card economics.
gaps_in_B: "FedNow adoption stories have mostly been about disbursements and B2B" may be true, but it is not in the supplied facts. B should label it as outside context, not settled ground.
"retail checkout" and "consumer checkout product" are more specific than the update allows. The facts say merchants can accept account-to-account payments; they do not describe checkout UX.

"The prevailing belief in the category is that pay-by-bank is a general-purpose card replacement" is an unsourced strawman. The contrarian math angle works without pretending a consensus was provided.

"Plaid needs 12,000 banks to help route payments past the fees banks collect" is sharp, but the bank-revenue premise is still an inference. B admits that later; the headline should carry the same discipline.
